course_description:
This course explores the legal, regulatory, economic and philosophical issues associated with human-animal relationships in contemporary society. As an indicator of societal maturity, how animals are used for work, companionship, entertainment, research and consumption raise complex legal, ethical and regulatory issues.

Adopting inter-disciplinary approaches, this course explores human-animal relationships through prevailing and traditional legal doctrines while inviting critique and evaluation through wider disciplines including philosophy, economics and science. Students will be challenged in their understanding of animals as they are traditionally conceptualised in law (including underlying philosophical assumptions) while critically evaluating how legal systems regulate and thus influence human-animal relationships.

course_aims:
Education Mission Statement

The mission of the School of Law is to educate you in and about the law. We seek to assist you to think critically about the law and to investigate its structures, principles, policies, and values. This is achieved by engaging with you as fellow investigators in a range of critical and intellectual conversations about the law and its place in society. Our role is thus to guide you in your own intellectual journey in the law and to equip you with the necessary skills that will enable you to continue that journey long after you have left the School.

Course Aims

This course introduces students to the legal, regulatory and ethical frameworks and issues associated with various forms of interaction between humans and animals in contemporary society. In doing so, the course aims to provide students with an opportunity for critical reflection and evaluation of different forms of human-animal interaction including animals as companions, as food, as entertainment, as resources and as 'pests'. The course will also provide introduction to international approaches to animal law enabling evaluation and critique of the Australian context. The course aims to enable students to articulate and defend their own views concerning human-animal relationships.

learning_outcomes.description: Recognise and explain the principal philosophical / ethical theories associated with the human-animal relationship.
Identify and understand the principal legal and regulatory frameworks by which human-animal relationships are managed.
Critically analyse the objectives of those legal and regulatory frameworks in light of both philosophical theories and international jurisprudence.
Understand how Commonwealth, State and Local Council laws and regulations are intended to work together in regulating animals.
Identify the rights and obligations imposed upon individuals and other legal entities under these Commonwealth, State and Local Council regulatory regimes as they relate to the treatment of animals.
Communicate effectively, appropriately and persuasively on issues concerning animal law and regulation.
Conduct legal research, undertake reasoned debate and engage in persuasive argument concerning animal law and regulation.

assessment_details.task_description: Each Thursday, a small set of readings (articles, cases or policy documents) will be posted to the Animal Law Blackboard site. During the first 30 minutes of the class on the following Thursday (commencing in Week 2), students will be asked to draft an open-book, 300-400 hand-written response to a question concerning those readings. The question will be provided at the start of that Thursday class. Responses will be collected and assigned a mark of up to 5%. Across the 12 weeks of the semester, students will be required to complete ten of these responses. At the end of the semester, the 7 highest results for each student will be counted for a maximum mark of 35%. Read full task description Hide full task description

You may be able to apply for an extension .

Extension to Assessment Due Date
The maximum extension for an assessment item due within the semester / teaching period in which the course is offered is 7 days. In exceptional circumstances, an extension may be approved for a further 7 days. Where a student is incapacitated for a period longer than 14 days, they are advised to apply for removal of course.

Additional information on extensions can be found within the Assessment Procedure .
Spoken or written notification of difficulties with assessment deadlines to a course coordinator or the School does not constitute an authorised extension.
Late submission
A penalty of 10% of the maximum possible mark will be deducted per 24 hours from time submission is due for up to 7 days. After 7 days, you will receive a mark of 0.
Penalties for Late Submission
The following penalties apply to late submission of an assessment item, assuming that an extension has not been approved, and that late submission is academically possible (e.g., it does not delay feedback to a cohort, or interfere with course delivery).
First 7 periods of 24 hours (or part thereof) - 10% per 24 hours of the maximum possible mark for the assessment item. For example, a report worth a maximum of 40 marks, submitted 28 hours late will attract a penalty of 8 marks, calculated as 2 periods of 24 hours x 10% x 40 marks.
More than 7 periods of 24 hours - 100%.

learning_activities.topic: Seminars Classes for Animal Law during Semester Two, 2026 are scheduled in "Seminar" format each Thursday from 5:00pm - 8:00pm. Each Thursday seminar will include between 3-4 activities. These activities will include (i) the presentation of material (by the instructor) relevant to the topic for the week; (ii) commencing in Week 2, writing the critical reflections about the set reading material, (iii) discussion and debate (led and moderated by the instructor) about the material relevant to the topic for the week, including relevant news items concerning animal law, (iv) commencing in Week 6, the oral presentations and associated questions and discussions. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05, L06, L07
